text: The Taliban released a biography of founder Mullah Mohammed Omar to dispel rumors of his death and reassert his leadership amid rising competition from ISIS. The document details Omar’s early life and current command structure, aiming to counter speculation that the reclusive leader has died or lost influence.

Hundreds of mourners gathered in South Carolina for the funeral of Walter Scott, whose fatal shooting by a police officer has sparked national debate on race and law enforcement. Former Officer Michael Slager faces murder charges after bystander video contradicted his initial account of the incident, though defense attorneys cite witness reports of a prior struggle. Family members and officials hailed Scott’s death as a catalyst for change while legal experts anticipate challenges to the murder charge based on claims of self-defense.

A former TSA agent received a six-month jail sentence and five-and-a-half years of probation for secretly videotaping a female co-worker in a restroom and burglarizing her home. Daniel Boykin pleaded guilty to unlawful photography, aggravated burglary, and computer violations after police discovered over 90 videos and 1,500 photos of the victim on his devices. The judge condemned the "egregious" invasion of privacy, while the TSA reaffirmed its zero-tolerance policy for employee misconduct following Boykin's termination.

Lacking conventional natural resources, Cape Verde is leveraging its rich musical heritage to drive economic growth and boost tourism. Initiatives like the Atlantic Music Expo and Kriol Jazz Festival aim to provide local artists with global exposure while attracting international visitors. Government and private sector leaders view this creative economy strategy as a vital alternative to traditional resource-based development.

Arsenal defeated Burnley 1-0 to narrow the Premier League title gap to four points ahead of next week's clash with leaders Chelsea. Aston Villa boosted their survival hopes with a win over Tottenham, while Crystal Palace thrashed Sunderland behind Yannick Bolasie's hat-trick.

Original *Twin Peaks* cast members have launched a #SaveTwinPeaks video campaign backing creator David Lynch amid his salary dispute with Showtime. The stars urge the network to retain Lynch, arguing the revival is incomplete without him following his Sunday announcement that he was exiting the project. Showtime maintains hope for a resolution while confirming only star Kyle MacLachlan for the planned 2016 reboot.

Andrew Getty, 47, grandson of oil tycoon J. Paul Getty, died of apparent natural causes at his Los Angeles home with no foul play suspected. Police cited several health issues and recovered medication from the scene, while an autopsy remains pending. The heir had recently sought a restraining order against an ex-girlfriend, citing a serious medical condition that made him vulnerable to stress-induced blood pressure spikes.

Maryland police stated Nyia Parler cannot be extradited to Philadelphia on charges of abandoning her quadriplegic son in the woods until she completes an unspecified medical treatment. Parler faces multiple assault and endangerment counts after allegedly leaving her disabled 21-year-old son in Cobbs Creek Park for four days while visiting a boyfriend. The victim was discovered dehydrated and malnourished but is currently recovering in a hospital under the care of relatives.

NASA astrophysicist Amy Mainzer has named asteroid 316201 "Malala" to honor Pakistani education activist Malala Yousafzai. The designation recognizes Yousafzai’s advocacy for girls' schooling and addresses the historical underrepresentation of women in celestial nomenclature.

The CDC reports 100 cases of gastrointestinal illness aboard the Celebrity Infinity, affecting both passengers and crew. Agency officials will board the vessel in San Diego to investigate the undetermined cause of the outbreak. This marks the third such incident for the ship, following previous outbreaks in 2006 and 2013.

The entire "Star Wars" saga hits digital HD this week, while "Vampire Diaries" star Nina Dobrev announces her departure from the CW series. Actor James Best, known for "The Dukes of Hazzard," dies alongside other Hollywood figures, and Mindy Kaling’s brother sparks controversy with claims he posed as Black to enter medical school.

The FBI charged a Philadelphia woman with attempting to travel to Syria to join ISIS, marking one of three terror-related arrests this week. Two New York women were also detained for allegedly plotting domestic explosive attacks. These cases highlight a surge in Justice Department prosecutions targeting individuals seeking to support foreign terrorist organizations.

HBO has released a teaser for the second season of "True Detective," starring Colin Farrell, Vince Vaughn, Rachel McAdams, and Taylor Kitsch. The new California-set narrative follows three law enforcement officers and a criminal entangled in conspiracy and betrayal. The critically acclaimed series returns on June 21.

Carlos Colina, 32, faces assault and improper disposal charges after human remains were found in a duffel bag and nearby apartment in Cambridge, Massachusetts. The victim was identified as 26-year-old Jonathan Camilien, an acquaintance of the suspect. Authorities continue to analyze evidence pending further medical examiner results.

Blue-chip basketball recruit Trey Moses asked high school freshman Ellie Meredith, who has Down syndrome, to prom in a viral gymnasium proposal. The gesture highlights the impact of Eastern High School’s Best Buddies program, which fosters friendships between students with and without developmental disabilities. Moses plans to major in special education at Ball State University, drawing praise from coaches and family for his character.

NBC premieres "A.D. The Bible Continues" Sunday, launching a 12-week sequel to the History Channel's hit miniseries just in time for Easter. Other notable debuts include the final season of AMC's "Mad Men," Louis C.K.'s return on FX, and Netflix's gritty "Daredevil" series.

Indiana Governor Mike Pence’s signing of a controversial religious freedom law is viewed as a strategic move to bolster his 2016 presidential credentials among ultraconservatives. The decision has ignited a national debate, forcing the Republican field further right and ensuring LGBT rights remain a central issue in the upcoming primary season.

Apple released a mobile OS update featuring diverse emoji options, including varied skin tones and same-sex couples, sparking mixed reactions regarding representation. While the move was praised for reflecting changing demographics, it drew criticism from some conservatives and left out groups like redheads and Armenians. The update marks a significant shift in digital inclusivity, though debates over cultural and political implications persist.

Avril Lavigne revealed she was bedridden for five months after contracting Lyme disease, dispelling rumors regarding rehab or pregnancy. The singer describes a severe battle with the tick-borne illness that left her unable to move or speak before beginning recovery. Now 80 percent better, Lavigne is releasing a new single and embracing a renewed perspective on life.

New research by the Anne Frank House indicates Anne and Margot Frank died at least a month earlier than the previously accepted March 1945 date. Analysis of survivor testimonies and medical records suggests the sisters likely perished in February 1945 from typhus, contradicting official Dutch records.

Two Troy University students face sexual battery charges for an alleged gang rape in Panama City Beach, Florida, after police discovered incriminating video during an unrelated investigation. The suspects have been suspended from the university and removed from athletic teams as authorities continue to probe the incident.

A Washington State dog named Theia survived a car accident, blunt force trauma, and burial to emerge from a field four days later with severe injuries. Her rescuer has raised over $10,000 for necessary surgeries, including jaw and sinus repairs, as the "miracle dog" recovers at a veterinary hospital.

The FBI has confirmed the death of Malaysian bomb maker Zulkifli bin Hir, known as Marwan, following DNA verification from a January raid in the southern Philippines. The operation resulted in the deaths of 44 elite police commandos and shattered a ceasefire with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front. Critics argue the high-cost mission jeopardized regional peace efforts for a target whose threat level may have been exaggerated.

The author criticizes the Obama administration's nuclear framework with Iran, arguing it surrenders crucial leverage by lifting sanctions while allowing Tehran to retain its nuclear infrastructure. The piece warns that weak inspection safeguards and short-term restrictions mirror failed past agreements, potentially enabling Iran to develop weapons while continuing to sponsor regional terrorism.

"Mad Men" returns for its final episodes, exploring the disintegration of 1960s social orders and the Sterling Cooper agency amid historical turmoil. Speculation centers on major character exits, including Roger Sterling’s potential demise and Peggy Olson’s rise, while Don Draper faces an existential reckoning. The series is expected to conclude with a poignant reflection on the era's end, leaving its iconic protagonist alone atop the changing zeitgeist.

Dallas Zoo giraffe Katie gave birth to a healthy 6-foot calf Friday during an hour-long labor streamed live by Animal Planet. The newborn showed positive signs of vitality, including moving ears and nursing attempts, following a standard 15-month gestation period.

Loretta Lynch’s historic nomination for attorney general faces a record-breaking Senate confirmation delay, sparking accusations of racial bias and partisan obstruction from Democrats. Republicans deny racial motives, attributing the stall to disputes over immigration policy and human trafficking legislation. Meanwhile, Lynch’s supporters in North Carolina intensify pressure on GOP senators to schedule a final vote.

Three people were killed and five wounded after armed assailants stormed the attorney general's office in northern Afghanistan's Balkh province. Afghan security forces remain engaged in an ongoing firefight with the attackers while working to rescue remaining hostages and minimize civilian casualties.

Bob Barker, 91, returned to "The Price Is Right" for the first time in eight years during the April 1 broadcast. The former host led the opening "Lucky Seven" segment before handing duties back to current host Drew Carey. Barker’s appearance marked a brief but seamless comeback for the television legend.

Blues legend B.B. King was discharged from the hospital Tuesday after being treated for dehydration linked to his Type II diabetes. The 89-year-old musician stated he is "feeling much better" and has returned home to rest with his family.

Following Dzhokhar Tsarnaev's conviction for the Boston Marathon bombing, this analysis argues that Islamic extremism stems from political grievances and perceived persecution rather than inherent religious doctrine. The author contends that combating radicalization requires addressing these root causes and empowering Muslim communities to reject violence through engagement, not theological reformation.

CNN highlights top videos featuring Mike Tyson's abandoned Ohio mansion, the world's fastest Fury 325 roller coaster, and sexual assault allegations against Bikram Choudhury. Additional segments include a Germanwings crash witness account, a debate on Indiana's religious freedom law, and a study on perceived facial beauty.

The Pentagon reports coalition forces have reclaimed 25-30% of ISIS-held Iraqi territory, though experts caution that insurgencies adapt rapidly to territorial losses. Analysts characterize the current strategy as a conventional frontal push rather than effective maneuver warfare, noting ISIS uses asymmetric attacks to distract from strategic setbacks.

Ottawa Fury FC player Oliver Minatel survived an alleged choking attempt by a fellow passenger on an Air Canada flight to Atlanta. The suspect, who claimed the team was trying to kill him, was escorted off the aircraft for medical and mental evaluation. The FBI is reviewing the incident, though no federal charges are currently pending.

Former banker Rurik Jutting faces two murder charges after the bodies of Indonesian women Seneng Mujiasih and Sumarti Ningsih were discovered in his Hong Kong apartment. A court hearing to determine if there is sufficient evidence for trial has been adjourned until May to allow for further forensic analysis.

One fatality was reported after multiple tornadoes swept through the Midwest on Thursday, causing widespread destruction in rural Illinois communities including Rochelle and Fairdale. While dozens of homes were flattened and significant property damage occurred, officials credited early warnings for limiting casualties to minor injuries outside the single death. Emergency responders continue to assess the devastation in Ogle County, where sheriff Brian VanVickle lost his own home but confirmed his family's safety.

Don McLean’s original manuscript for "American Pie" sold for $1.2 million at a Christie's auction, marking the third-highest price ever paid for an American literary manuscript. The 70-year-old singer-songwriter authorized the sale to secure financial stability for his family, noting that the 16-page draft includes extensive notes and unused lyrics. This transaction trails only Bob Dylan’s "Like a Rolling Stone" manuscript, which previously set the record for popular music manuscripts at $2 million.

UNRWA Commissioner-General Pierre Krähenbühl will conduct an emergency visit to Syria’s Yarmouk refugee camp Saturday to assess the dire humanitarian crisis facing 18,000 trapped civilians. The mission addresses deepening concerns over safety and aid shortages in the camp, which remains under the control of armed groups and has been largely cut off since 2013.

Saudi-led airstrikes in Yemen have killed approximately 600 people and crippled infrastructure, prompting urgent calls from the ICRC for a humanitarian ceasefire to deliver critical aid. Meanwhile, the UN Security Council failed to reach a decision on a Russian-drafted resolution to halt the bombing campaign as ground fighting intensifies. The escalating conflict has also allowed al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula to expand its territorial control amidst the chaos.

Legendary Australian cricketer and broadcaster Richie Benaud has died at age 84 following a battle with skin cancer. Revered as the "voice of cricket," Benaud was celebrated for his undefeated captaincy record and decades of iconic BBC commentary. Tributes have poured in from global leaders and sporting figures, honoring his profound impact on the game.

Western North America witnessed the century's shortest total lunar eclipse, lasting just under five minutes during a rare "tetrad" series. While viewers west of the Mississippi enjoyed the full event, sunrise obscured the view on the East Coast, with partial visibility across much of the nation and select global regions.

Federal prosecutors have charged real estate heir Robert Durst with unlawful firearm possession after authorities discovered a revolver in his New Orleans hotel room. The 71-year-old, currently held without bail on a first-degree murder charge for the 2000 killing of Susan Berman, faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted on the new federal count. Durst awaits extradition to Los Angeles while his defense cites serious health issues, including hydrocephalus and cancer, amid ongoing FBI scrutiny of other cold cases linked to him.

"Furious 7" releases Friday, serving as a poignant tribute to late star Paul Walker following his 2013 death during production. Filmmakers utilized script rewrites and body doubles to complete Walker's arc, retiring his character rather than killing him off. Co-star Vin Diesel and Walker's family have praised the film's emotional farewell, which honors the actor's legacy and humility.

"The Price Is Right" model Manuela Arbelaez accidentally revealed the correct answer for a new car, prompting host Drew Carey to award the prize. The blunder occurred during a busy week for the show that also featured a surprise appearance by former host Bob Barker.

Thai Smile has unveiled a new Airbus A320 featuring "Adventure Time" characters on its exterior and interior. The themed aircraft results from a partnership with Cartoon Network Amazone and will launch service between Bangkok and Phuket on April 4.

Pedestrians in Washington, D.C., halted traffic and used an umbrella to guide a mother duck and her brood across a busy street on Tuesday. The group safely escorted the birds to a nearby grassy area after they caused a stir among locals and media crews.

French investigators have concluded evidence collection at the Germanwings Flight 9525 crash site, having recovered both flight recorders and isolated 150 DNA profiles. Authorities confirmed co-pilot Andreas Lubitz intentionally crashed the plane after locking the captain out of the cockpit, citing his concealed history of depression and unfitness for work.

Cuba makes its historic debut at the Summit of the Americas as the U.S. ends a decades-long blockade on its attendance, marking a significant thaw in diplomatic relations. However, tensions persist over Cuba’s state sponsor of terrorism designation and its alliance with Venezuela, complicating efforts to fully restore ties. While street clashes marred the opening, polls indicate strong Cuban public support for improved relations with Washington.

Despite teachings on the perils of wealth, Jesus’ ministry relied on financial support from affluent followers, including women like Mary Magdalene and Joanna. These patrons provided essential resources that sustained the itinerant group at a subsistence level throughout their mission.

The California Public Utilities Commission ordered Pacific Gas & Electric to pay a record $1.6 billion penalty for unsafe gas pipeline operations linked to the fatal 2010 San Bruno explosion. Most of the fine mandates infrastructure safety improvements, marking the largest utility penalty in state history. PG&E expressed remorse and highlighted ongoing safety upgrades while accepting responsibility for the tragedy that killed eight people.

Lauren Hill, the 19-year-old college basketball player who inspired millions in her fight against terminal brain cancer, died Friday. The NCAA previously expedited Mount St. Joseph University's season opener to allow Hill to fulfill her dream of playing a collegiate game. Her legacy includes raising $1.4 million for pediatric cancer research and leaving a global message of resilience and hope.

A massive fire erupted Friday morning at General Electric’s Appliance Park in Louisville, Kentucky, sending thick smoke across the industrial area. Authorities reported no injuries as firefighters battled the multi-alarm blaze, though the cause remains unknown.

Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, hailed as a hero for securing a nuclear breakthrough with the U.S., holds a complex history including U.S. education and past revolutionary activism. Despite previous Justice Department investigations into his alleged ties to sanctions-busting entities, Zarif remains central to ongoing negotiations aimed at finalizing a deal by June 30.

A Connecticut judge denied a motion to release 17-year-old Hodgkin lymphoma patient "Cassandra C." from state custody, keeping her in temporary care despite her remission status. The ruling blocks the teen's return home and visitation rights, with officials citing prior flight risks until her chemotherapy concludes in late April. Attorneys for Cassandra and her mother expressed disappointment and are considering an appeal against the decision.

New psychological analysis confirms William Shakespeare and John Fletcher authored the 1728 play "Double Falsehood," largely debunking claims that publisher Lewis Theobald forged the work. Researchers used computer software to compare linguistic patterns, finding a decisive match with Shakespeare’s style in the first half and a shared signature with Fletcher in the second. While experts praise the study's objectivity, some scholars caution that the debate over the play's provenance may persist among skeptics.

French prosecutors denied the existence of an onboard video from the Germanwings crash, contradicting media reports while confirming co-pilot Andreas Lubitz had a history of severe depression. Lufthansa acknowledged it knew of Lubitz's prior mental health struggles during his training, as investigators explore fears over his medical fitness as a potential motive. Recovery teams continue searching the French Alps site, with officials expecting to identify all 150 victims via DNA analysis by week's end.

Decorated veteran Emy Afalava and fellow American Samoans challenge their non-citizen status in federal court, arguing the 14th Amendment guarantees birthright citizenship. The lawsuit targets a legal exception rooted in early 20th-century racial precedents that denies full constitutional rights to residents of the U.S. territory. Plaintiffs seek to overturn this disparity, noting American Samoans remain the only inhabitants of U.S. island territories without automatic citizenship.

Blue Bell Creameries has temporarily closed its Broken Arrow, Oklahoma plant and issued a recall for specific 3-ounce ice cream servings after listeria contamination was detected. The CDC warned consumers to discard affected products linked to the facility, marking the company's first-ever recall amid ongoing investigations into separate listeria outbreaks in Kansas and Texas.

Al-Shabaab has claimed responsibility for a deadly attack on Garissa University College in Kenya, marking a significant escalation in the group's cross-border terrorism. The incident underscores deteriorating security in East Africa, driven by radical ideology and deep-seated regional instability including governance failures and social exclusion. Experts warn that lasting peace requires addressing these root causes alongside direct military countermeasures.

The U.S. is lodging a formal diplomatic complaint with Moscow after a Russian SU-27 intercepted an American RC-135U reconnaissance plane in international airspace over the Baltic Sea. The Pentagon condemned the Russian pilot's aggressive maneuvers as "unsafe and unprofessional," while dismissing Russian claims that the U.S. aircraft had its transponder switched off. This incident marks the latest in a series of tense aerial encounters between the two nations, echoing a dangerous close pass in the Pacific last year.

Artist Phillip Hyman created a black-winged angel sculpture from reclaimed wood to mourn Walter Scott, the unarmed man killed by police in North Charleston. The artwork has since become a prominent icon for Black Lives Matter protesters, who display it at rallies to highlight the tragedy and demand justice.

North Charleston Officer Michael Slager has been fired and charged with murder after bystander video contradicted his claim that he shot Walter Scott in self-defense. The footage shows Slager firing eight times at the unarmed, fleeing man and later appearing to plant a Taser near the body. Initial police reports alleging Scott seized the weapon have been discredited by the visual evidence and witness testimony.

ISIS claims to have seized parts of Iraq's Baiji oil refinery, though government officials deny the assertion and maintain full control. The strategic facility near Tikrit has seen repeated clashes, with independent verification of the latest assault currently unavailable.

Nashville's ban on offering female sterilization in plea deals has sparked debate over the practice's constitutionality and historical ties to eugenics. The author argues that such voluntary waivers of Eighth Amendment rights are likely legal, noting that similar procedures for male offenders have long gone unchallenged. Public outrage appears driven by gender bias rather than legal precedent, as society tolerates male castration but rejects female sterilization.

The historic Ebola epidemic has infected over 25,000 people and killed more than 10,000, exposing critical flaws in global public health systems. While weekly cases have dropped to their lowest level since May 2014, unsafe burials and unidentified transmission chains in Guinea threaten to sustain the outbreak.

The NCAA denies legal responsibility for ensuring academic integrity at member institutions in a court filing responding to a lawsuit over the University of North Carolina’s academic fraud scandal. This stance contradicts the organization’s public rhetoric prioritizing student-athlete education and mirrors previous denials of duty regarding player health and safety. Critics condemn the position as hypocritical, while the NCAA argues it lacks operational control over individual university courses.

An explosion and subsequent fire at a paraxylene plant in Fujian province injured six people, though authorities report no toxic chemical spill. Over 600 firefighters brought the blaze under control after an oil leak triggered the Monday night incident. The facility has faced public opposition over pollution concerns since its relocation from Xiamen in 2007.

The fatal shooting of Walter Scott underscores the critical need for police body cameras to ensure accountability and deter misconduct. While such devices cannot eradicate systemic racial bias, they offer an immediate mechanism to restore public trust and reduce use-of-force incidents. Implementing widespread camera usage serves as a vital interim solution while society addresses deeper structural inequalities.

The VII Summit of Americas’ focus on historic U.S.-Cuba rapprochement has been overshadowed by escalating tensions between Washington and Caracas. Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro condemned new U.S. sanctions as a threat to national security, drawing public support from Cuban officials. This diplomatic rift threatens to disrupt the hemisphere's gathering, turning a celebratory event into a contentious political standoff.

A fire broke out in the rubber insulation of a nuclear submarine undergoing repairs at Russia's Zvyozdochka shipyard. Officials confirmed no injuries occurred and stated there was no risk to personnel, as the vessel contained no nuclear fuel or armaments.

The Philippines has issued flash flood and landslide warnings as weakened Tropical Storm Maysak, locally named Chedeng, approaches with sustained winds exceeding 70 mph. Authorities have enforced precautionary evacuations and banned coastal activities ahead of the storm's expected Sunday landfall in Isabela province.

NFL legend Deion Sanders publicly rebuked his son on Twitter for claiming to eat only "hood doughnuts," reminding the SMU receiver of his trust fund and "Well Off" clothing line. Sanders urged his son to drop the affectation, citing their family's wealth with hashtags like #Huxtable and #Trustfund. Deion Sanders Jr. accepted the critique in stride, retweeting his father's comments without deletion.

Guatemala faces an epidemic of gender-based violence and femicide, driven by a legacy of civil war impunity, entrenched machismo, and a weak judicial system. Despite high homicide rates and institutional failures, grassroots initiatives and new legal frameworks are slowly empowering survivors to seek justice and challenge deep-rooted patriarchal norms.

Police in Malegaon, India, are mandating identity cards and photographs for cattle to enforce a strict state ban on beef consumption and cow slaughter. Authorities aim to create a database to quickly verify livestock status and solve crimes, following recent arrests and tougher penalties under the Maharashtra Animal Preservation Bill. The move has sparked protests from beef traders and civil liberties advocates, who argue against government interference in personal dietary choices.

Lucknow police in northern India have acquired pepper-spraying drones to disperse violent crowds and mob attacks. The initiative has sparked debate over civil liberties, with critics condemning the move as an authoritarian alternative to dialogue and mediation. Officials plan to officially launch the surveillance and crowd-control program later this month.

Don McLean's original handwritten lyrics for "American Pie" sold for $1.2 million at Christie's auction house on Tuesday. The 16-page manuscript of the 1971 cultural anthem was purchased by an unnamed buyer.

London's Hatton Garden vault heist marks a rare return to physical burglary, contrasting with modern cybercrime trends. Former Scotland Yard commander Roy Ramm attributes such sophisticated raids to meticulous planning, inside information, and financial motive rather than thrill-seeking. Investigators are now focusing on forensic evidence and potential insider involvement to track the gang.

7-Eleven is hosting its first Bring-Your-Own-Cup Slurpee Day this Saturday, allowing U.S. customers to fill sanitary containers for $1.49. Participants may use creative vessels like trophies or buckets, provided they fit through a 10-inch display hole. The promotion aims to kick off peak Slurpee season and differs from the chain's traditional July freebie event.

Kentucky’s first female and Black state senator condemns Rand Paul’s presidential bid, citing his opposition to the Civil Rights Act and Voting Rights Act as evidence of regressive policies. She argues that despite GOP outreach efforts, Paul’s record on minority issues and social programs disqualifies him from leading the nation. The op-ed concludes that his campaign rhetoric fails to mask a platform that threatens decades of democratic progress.

A passenger died and the driver sustained minor injuries after a Lamborghini crashed into a guardrail at Walt Disney World Speedway’s Exotic Driving Experience on Sunday. Florida Highway Patrol identified the victim as 36-year-old Gary Terry, while operator Petty Holdings issued a statement expressing sympathy for those involved in the fatal accident.

Former NFL star Aaron Hernandez’s defense rested its case Monday after a brief presentation, setting the stage for closing arguments and jury deliberations in his murder trial. Prosecutors relied on circumstantial evidence, including disputed footprint analysis and security footage, to link Hernandez to the 2013 shooting death of Odin Lloyd. The former Patriot faces additional murder charges in a separate Boston case, though those allegations remain excluded from this trial.

Chinese authorities have formally detained five women's rights activists for "creating disturbances" after they planned an International Women's Day protest against sexual harassment. The detentions, which deny the women access to legal counsel and medical care, coincide with Beijing's preparations to adopt its first anti-domestic violence law. A critical April 13 deadline looms for the activists' release or formal arrest, highlighting a broader government crackdown on independent civil society groups.

Former Maryland Governor Martin O'Malley challenged Hillary Clinton's perceived inevitability in Iowa, citing historical precedents where frontrunners lost nominations. While acknowledging Clinton’s qualifications, O'Malley argued for a robust Democratic primary, stating it would be an "extreme poverty" to have only one candidate. The remarks come as Clinton prepares to officially launch her presidential bid amid polling leads of over 40 points.

Ursula Ward delivered an emotional victim impact statement following the first-degree murder conviction and life sentence of former NFL player Aaron Hernandez for the 2013 killing of her son, Odin Lloyd. Family members described Lloyd as a devoted brother and hard worker, with Ward expressing profound grief while ultimately offering forgiveness to those involved in his death.

Ted Cruz launched his presidential campaign in Iowa by aggressively courting the state's influential evangelical base through religious rhetoric and staunch defense of religious liberty laws. The Texas senator aims to unite social conservatives with libertarian and Tea Party factions, seeking to boost evangelical turnout to 2004 levels. This strategy positions Cruz against a crowded GOP field where rivals like Huckabee, Santorum, and Carson are also vying for the critical religious vote.

Marvel Studios unveiled Paul Bettany as Vision in a new "Avengers: Age of Ultron" poster, ending months of speculation about the android's appearance. The studio also released the first official look at Charlie Cox’s Daredevil suit ahead of the Netflix series premiere. Concurrently, 20th Century Fox announced Ben Hardy as Angel for "X-Men: Apocalypse" and revealed Jamie Bell’s CGI-rendered Thing for the "Fantastic Four" reboot.

The Italian Coast Guard rescued 978 migrants off Libya on Friday, adding to over 10,000 arrivals in Italy during the first quarter of 2015. The International Organization for Migration reports at least 480 deaths in the Mediterranean this year, a sharp increase from the previous year, as desperate asylum seekers flee conflict and poverty.

French network TV5Monde regained partial control of its broadcasts and social media Thursday following a severe cyberattack that crippled operations the previous day. Although ISIS imagery appeared on hijacked accounts, no group has officially claimed responsibility for the intrusion. The outage disrupted service to millions of viewers across 11 channels before engineers began restoring access.

Director David Lynch has withdrawn from directing the "Twin Peaks" revival, citing insufficient funding to produce the series properly. Showtime expressed sadness over the decision but remains hopeful that Lynch and co-creator Mark Frost will still helm the project. The network confirmed the third season will proceed, with star Kyle MacLachlan set to reprise his role.

High-profile trials for Aaron Hernandez and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev reach critical stages in Massachusetts as closing arguments and jury deliberations begin. Senator Rand Paul officially launches his presidential bid, while Chicago voters decide a mayoral runoff between Rahm Emanuel and Jesus Garcia. Meanwhile, Ferguson, Missouri holds local elections under the shadow of ongoing protests regarding police representation and Michael Brown’s death.

Tornado sirens blared across Kansas and Missouri on Wednesday night as severe storms spawned multiple twisters, causing wind damage and flooding. Experts warned of the heightened danger from nighttime tornadoes while forecasting additional severe weather for the Midwest and surrounding regions on Thursday.

Jodi Arias was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of release Monday for the 2008 murder of her ex-boyfriend, Travis Alexander. Maricopa County Judge Sherry Stephens imposed the maximum penalty after two separate juries failed to reach a unanimous decision on the death sentence. Arias expressed remorse during the hearing, while Alexander’s family delivered emotional victim impact statements.

The EPA confirmed methyl bromide exposure likely sickened a Delaware family at a U.S. Virgin Islands luxury villa, prompting an ongoing investigation into potential regulatory violations. The Department of Justice has launched a criminal probe involving pest control firm Terminix, whose parent company disclosed the inquiry in an SEC filing.

A Columbia University review confirmed institutional failures at Rolling Stone regarding its flawed UVA gang rape story, prompting an apology from the magazine. While the university is barred from suing for defamation, Phi Kappa Psi fraternity members may pursue legal action by arguing the "small group" exception applies to their case. Success hinges on proving individualized financial harm and overcoming defenses regarding the group's size and fluidity.

FBI agents shot and captured suspected serial robber Kevone Charleston in Georgia after a high-speed chase involving multiple vehicle collisions. Two agents sustained non-life-threatening injuries during the confrontation, which ended an investigation into 32 commercial robberies.

Alaska Airlines Flight 448 returned to Seattle shortly after takeoff when a sleeping ramp agent trapped in the cargo hold banged for help. The employee, who had fallen asleep during loading, was unharmed and later discharged from a hospital. Alaska Airlines is investigating the incident involving the Menzies Aviation contractor.

A North Carolina judge ruled Monday that Craig Hicks is eligible for the death penalty in connection with the February shootings of three Muslim college students in Chapel Hill. Hicks faces three counts of first-degree murder, while federal authorities continue a parallel inquiry into whether the killings constituted a hate crime.

Amnesty International urges Afghan authorities to protect women's rights activists facing persecution from the Taliban, warlords, and government officials. The call follows the brutal mob killing of Farkhunda in Kabul, which sparked unprecedented female-led protests despite a 20% rise in women's deaths last year. Activists warn that continued state inaction and impunity for perpetrators threaten to reverse hard-won gains for women in the country.

A New York judge authorized serving divorce papers via Facebook private message, marking a shift from traditional in-person delivery to digital methods for evasive defendants. This ruling highlights the legal system's adaptation to modern connectivity, prioritizing reliable electronic notification over antiquated alternatives like publication or "nail and mail" service.

Rev. Robert H. Schuller, founder of the Crystal Cathedral and "Hour of Power" televangelism ministry, died Thursday at age 88 following a battle with esophageal cancer. The pioneering preacher rose from humble beginnings to build a massive religious empire known for its "possibility thinking" message before financial struggles and family succession disputes led to bankruptcy.

Four workers died and 45 were injured in a massive fire on Pemex's Abkatun Permanente oil rig off Mexico's coast Wednesday. Authorities evacuated approximately 300 personnel and extinguished the blaze by nightfall, confirming no structural collapse or oil spill occurred. The cause of the fire, which originated in the platform's dehydration and pumping area, remains under investigation.

Kansas Governor Sam Brownback signed the nation's first law banning "dismemberment abortion," a measure targeting the common second-trimester dilation and evacuation procedure. The legislation, which includes exceptions for maternal health, drew sharp condemnation from reproductive rights groups as the most restrictive in the U.S. while being hailed by anti-abortion advocates as a transformative policy precedent.

Kentucky guard Andrew Harrison apologized for using a racial slur against Wisconsin's Frank Kaminsky, claiming the remark was made in jest. Kaminsky accepted the apology and dismissed the incident after the two players spoke privately. The resolution comes just before Wisconsin faces Duke in the national championship game.

"Arrested Development" executive producer Brian Grazer confirmed the series will return for a fifth season of 17 episodes. Netflix declined to verify the announcement, and it remains unclear if the full original cast will reprise their roles.

CERN has successfully restarted the Large Hadron Collider following a two-year shutdown, with particle beams circulating inside the 17-mile ring. The world's largest physics experiment aims to recreate Big Bang conditions to investigate dark matter, antimatter, and the origins of mass. Scientists plan to increase beam energies to record levels in upcoming phases to address gaps in the Standard Model of particle physics.

An Iranian observation aircraft flew within 50 yards of a U.S. Navy helicopter in the Persian Gulf, prompting concerns that local commanders may be acting without central authorization. The unsafe maneuver occurred during sensitive nuclear negotiations and contrasts with recent professional Iranian conduct, leading U.S. officials to consider a formal protest. Intelligence suggests the pilot was likely reprimanded by higher-ups after the incident, as the aircraft disappeared from radar for two weeks.

Jurors convicted Dzhokhar Tsarnaev on all 30 counts, including 17 capital charges, in the Boston Marathon bombing trial. The case now moves to a penalty phase where the jury will determine if the 21-year-old faces execution. Legal analysts describe the defense's upcoming task of sparing Tsarnaev's life as an "uphill battle."

Indian police arrested four FabIndia employees for voyeurism after Education Minister Smriti Irani discovered a surveillance camera monitoring a changing room at a Goa store. Authorities confirmed the device could capture images of customers and have charged the staff, who face up to three years in prison if convicted. The retailer has sealed the outlet and pledged full cooperation with the ongoing investigation.

Iran plans to lift its decades-old ban on women attending men's sports events, with Deputy Sports Minister Abdolhamid Ahmadi announcing the change will take effect within the next year. The partial reversal, initially targeting indoor sports, follows intense international pressure from FIFA and recent diplomatic setbacks for the nation.

Former Satyam chairman Ramalinga Raju and nine others were sentenced to seven years in prison for orchestrating India's largest corporate fraud. The conviction stems from a $1.6 billion accounting scandal involving inflated profits and fictitious assets that rocked the software giant in 2009.

Alaska Airlines apologized and refunded tickets after removing cancer patient Elizabeth Sedway from a Hawaii flight for lacking a medical clearance note. The carrier admitted the situation was mishandled, acknowledging that while employee concern for passenger well-being prompted the removal, the execution caused significant disruption to Sedway’s treatment schedule.

Turkish singer-songwriter Kayahan died of cancer in Istanbul on Friday at age 66, five days after his birthday. The Eurovision contestant and guitarist rose to fame with his 1991 album "I Made a Vow" and was mourned by Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu for his lasting impact on Turkish music.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the Iran nuclear framework as a "bad deal" that fails to dismantle Tehran's nuclear infrastructure, urging increased pressure instead. President Obama and Energy Secretary Ernest Moniz defended the agreement as a necessary step to block pathways to a bomb, while Republican critics argued it grants Iran excessive flexibility. The dispute has intensified partisan tensions in Washington, with lawmakers debating whether to submit the final accord to Congress for approval.

A domestic kidnapping suspect shot a Census Bureau guard in Maryland before leading police on a chase into Washington, D.C., where he exchanged gunfire with officers. The pursuit ended in a crash and shootout on H Street that wounded both the suspect and a police officer. Authorities confirmed the kidnapping victim was recovered in good condition, while the injured guard remains in critical condition.

Imprisoned soldier Chelsea Manning has joined Twitter, dictating posts via a third-party firm due to prison restrictions on internet access. Manning, serving a 35-year sentence for the WikiLeaks leak, aims to engage in two-way conversation with her followers despite her confinement.

Hip-hop artist Nelly was arrested in Tennessee on felony drug charges after troopers discovered methamphetamine, marijuana, and multiple handguns during a search of his tour bus. The stop occurred on Interstate 40 when an officer noticed missing regulatory stickers and detected the odor of marijuana emanating from the vehicle. Nelly posted bond and was released from Putnam County Jail following the incident.

A Delaware father and his two sons remain hospitalized in critical or stable condition after suspected methyl bromide poisoning at a U.S. Virgin Islands villa, while the mother has been released. The EPA confirmed the presence of the restricted, odorless pesticide at the rental unit, prompting a criminal investigation by the Department of Justice. The resort’s pest control contractor has terminated its agreement with the property management company as authorities determine liability for the illegal indoor application.

Online dissent in Asia faces intensifying state repression, with governments in Singapore, Vietnam, and China utilizing defamation laws and imprisonment to silence bloggers. Meanwhile, weak rule of law in Bangladesh has led to the fatal hacking deaths of critics addressing religious issues. These trends highlight the growing vulnerability of digital journalists to both legal persecution and extrajudicial violence across the region.

Nina Dobrev announced her departure from "The Vampire Diaries" after six seasons, sparking backlash from fans concerned about the show's continuation and the fate of the "Delena" romance. While producer Julie Plec voiced full support for Dobrev's decision to pursue new opportunities, many viewers expressed anger and disappointment over the impending exit. Dobrev urged fans to remain engaged through the season finale in May, hinting at unexpected developments before her final episode.

Syria’s Yarmouk camp faces catastrophic destruction and a humanitarian crisis as government shelling and factional fighting trap approximately 18,000 Palestinian residents. ISIS incursions and subsequent battles with Jabhat al-Nusra have intensified the siege, cutting off aid and leaving civilians without food or water. Despite relentless violence and dwindling numbers, remaining inhabitants refuse to flee, vowing to stay in the devastated neighborhood.

NASA scientists project that while primitive life is likely abundant across the Milky Way's estimated 40 billion habitable-zone planets, intelligent civilizations remain statistically rare and temporally isolated. Upcoming missions, including the James Webb Space Telescope, will prioritize detecting atmospheric biosignatures on exoplanets and subsurface oceans within our solar system over searching for communicative beings. Consequently, the discovery of simple extraterrestrial life appears imminent, but meaningful contact with advanced intelligence remains highly improbable in the near future.

Massachusetts man Carlos Colina faces murder charges after human remains identified as 26-year-old Jonathan Camilien were found in a duffel bag and nearby apartment complex. Authorities linked Colina to the victim through surveillance footage, noting the two were acquainted. A judge has revoked Colina's bail in an unrelated assault case pending his April 14 arraignment.

Kanye West has settled a civil lawsuit with photographer Daniel Ramos, ending the case just before trial with an apology and a handshake. The dispute stemmed from a 2013 airport altercation where West assaulted Ramos, for which the rapper previously received probation and community service. Settlement terms were not disclosed, though attorney Gloria Allred emphasized the outcome reinforces that celebrities are not above the law.

President Obama’s political stake in securing an Iran nuclear deal has weakened the U.S. negotiating position, allowing Tehran to retain significant nuclear infrastructure while gaining immediate sanctions relief. Critics argue the resulting framework agreement fails to dismantle Iran’s program or ensure regional stability, effectively rewarding Iranian intransigence and alarming Arab allies. Consequently, the deal is viewed as a strategic victory for Iran that prioritizes Obama’s legacy over robust non-proliferation safeguards.

The fatal shooting of Walter Scott by Officer Michael Slager highlights the critical role of bystander video in securing accountability, as initial police reports contradicted the footage. However, the incident underscores a broader systemic failure: a 1994 federal law mandating comprehensive data collection on police use of force has been largely ignored for two decades. Consequently, the nation lacks reliable statistics on police killings, hindering efforts to address potential racial bias and excessive force.

Five U.S. clinicians monitored for Ebola exposure in an Omaha hospital have been released after testing negative for the virus. The aid workers, who treated patients in Sierra Leone, completed a 21-day observation period without developing symptoms. Their discharge leaves only a handful of remaining monitors expected to be cleared by federal health officials this week.

Mark Ronson’s “Uptown Funk!” rules the Billboard Hot 100 for a 13th week, becoming the decade's longest-leading hit and joining an elite group of singles with at least 13 weeks at No. 1. The track simultaneously tops Digital, Radio, and Streaming charts, maintaining a significant lead over runner-up Maroon 5’s “Sugar.” Newcomer Natalie La Rose enters the top 10 with her debut single “Somebody,” featuring Jeremih.

While "Lost" fans marked April 8, cinephiles celebrated "Rex Manning Day" from the 1995 film "Empire Records." The article highlights other cinematic dates, including "Titanic's" April 14, "Miss Congeniality's" April 25, and "Mean Girls'" October 3. It also notes the upcoming October 21, 2015 destination date from "Back to the Future Part II."

Critically panned biopic "Grace of Monaco" will bypass U.S. theaters to premiere on Lifetime this Memorial Day following poor international performance. Distributor The Weinstein Co. opted for the cable deal after the film faced backlash from Grace Kelly’s family and a public feud between director Olivier Dahan and Harvey Weinstein.

Tokyo's Shibuya ward passed an ordinance issuing partnership certificates to same-sex couples, granting limited rights such as hospital visitation and joint tenancy. Although not legally binding under national law, the move marks a significant symbolic step toward marriage equality in socially conservative Japan. Neighboring Setagaya ward has indicated it may follow suit as public support for LGBT rights grows among younger demographics.

California’s historic drought has triggered mandatory water cuts and raised national produce prices, while severe dryness in Texas and Oklahoma drove up beef costs. Although the crisis impacts tourism and agriculture across the West, California wine quality and supply remain robust despite the arid conditions.

The University of Michigan reversed its decision to cancel a screening of "American Sniper," citing a commitment to freedom of expression after student backlash. Vice President E. Royster Harper admitted the initial cancellation was a mistake and confirmed the film will proceed as part of the UMix social series. An alternative screening of "Paddington" will be offered for students who prefer not to attend.

The 2015 MTV Movie Awards featured standout moments including Channing Tatum’s twerking and Amy Schumer’s sharp monologue, alongside musical collaborations from Fall Out Boy and Fetty Wap. However, the ceremony suffered misfires such as Schumer’s botched archery stunt, an awkward "Gone Girl" joke, and a rambling acceptance speech by Shailene Woodley.

Oregon officials towed a suspected tsunami debris fragment from Japan to Newport, discovering live yellowtail jack fish inside the hull. Biologists deemed the invasive species threat minimal, and the boat remains will be sent to a landfill. The fish have been transferred to the Oregon Coast Aquarium for care.

One year after Boko Haram abducted 276 Nigerian schoolgirls in Chibok, over 200 remain missing despite global outrage and the #BringBackOurGirls campaign. President-elect Muhammadu Buhari marked the anniversary with pledges to aggressively combat the militants, who continue to control significant territory and perpetrate violence. The unresolved crisis contributed to the defeat of incumbent President Goodluck Jonathan, while families endure ongoing grief and uncertainty.

Easter remains distinct from commercialized holidays by centering on the Holy Week Triduum, a three-day progression from Good Friday’s suffering through Holy Saturday’s limbo to Easter Sunday’s resurrection. This ritual mirrors the universal human experience of moving through darkness and anxiety toward transformation and hope. Consequently, the holiday offers a spiritual framework for understanding life’s inevitable cycles of loss and renewal.

Kenya has frozen 86 bank accounts linked to suspected Al-Shabaab supporters following the Garissa university massacre that killed 147 people. The government also launched airstrikes against militant training camps in Somalia and offered a reward for information on the attack's alleged organizer. These measures come amid heavy criticism of the security response and ongoing mourning for the victims, mostly students.

Former tech entrepreneur Jia Jiang launched the viral "100 Days of Rejection" project to conquer his fear of saying no, documenting bizarre public requests like Olympic-ring donuts. The initiative spawned a new book, "Rejection Proof," which reframes rejection as a manageable numbers game rather than a personal failure. Jiang now teaches others to embrace refusal as an opportunity for growth and resilience.

Attorney General Eric Holder issued a memo strictly prohibiting all Justice Department personnel from soliciting prostitutes, regardless of local legality. The directive aims to curb human trafficking demand and follows an inspector general report detailing misconduct by DEA agents abroad. Violations will result in suspension or termination, applying to employees at all times, including off-duty hours.

Authorities are investigating the fatal shooting of a Wayne Community College employee as a potential hate crime after arresting suspect Kenneth Morgan Stancil III in Florida. Stancil, a former work-study student dismissed for poor attendance, allegedly killed print shop operator Ron Lane with a shotgun before fleeing the North Carolina campus. Police are examining links to white supremacist groups, though both victim and suspect are white.

Amnesty International’s annual report reveals a global decline in executions to 607 in 2014, despite a surge in death sentences driven by political instability in Egypt and Nigeria. However, the review condemns a troubling trend of governments in China, Pakistan, and Indonesia exploiting capital punishment as a cynical, ineffective response to terrorism and crime. The organization urges world leaders to abandon the death penalty, noting that most nations have already abolished the practice.

A Duke University student admitted to hanging a noose near the student union and has been removed from campus pending a conduct review. The incident sparked protests and a university forum, with officials condemning the act as cowardly while criminal investigations continue. This event follows a series of recent racist incidents at other U.S. colleges.

Emmy-winning actor Richard Dysart, best known for his role as Leland McKenzie in "L.A. Law," has died at age 86 following a long illness. The veteran stage and screen performer passed away Sunday at his Santa Monica home, leaving behind a prolific career that included Broadway acclaim and numerous film and television roles.

Pope Francis led Easter Mass at the Vatican, urging global peace while Orthodox Christians in Jerusalem observed separate rites due to calendar differences. The holiday's shifting date stems from ancient lunar calculations linking it to Passover and the vernal equinox. Meanwhile, secular traditions like the Easter bunny and egg coloring persist alongside these religious observances.

Comedian Chris Rock sparked online debate by tweeting photos of three recent traffic stops, highlighting racial profiling concerns amid heightened national scrutiny of police conduct. The posts drew mixed reactions, including actor Isaiah Washington’s controversial advice to drive less conspicuous cars to avoid being pulled over. This incident echoes Rock’s long-standing comedic commentary on the disparities in how black and white drivers are treated by law enforcement.

Lynyrd Skynyrd's original drummer Robert Lewis Burns Jr. died Friday in a single-vehicle crash in Cartersville, Georgia, after striking a mailbox and tree while unrestrained. The 64-year-old musician, who left the band in 1975 prior to their famous 1977 plane crash, was remembered by surviving members for his humor and talent.

A viral photo of a cat on stairs has ignited online debate over whether the animal is ascending or descending, echoing previous optical illusion controversies. The image spread rapidly via Imgur and 9gag, prompting widespread social media discussion regarding perspective and motion. Advertisers have already begun leveraging the trending topic to engage audiences.

The U.S. and P5+1 partners secured a framework agreement with Iran in Lausanne that curbs its nuclear program to prevent weapons development through strict limits and permanent inspections. Critics in Congress face rebuttal on claims regarding the deal's objectives, scope, and durability, as experts affirm the accord effectively blocks covert arsenal creation. Rejecting the agreement risks unraveling international sanctions and NATO cohesion without addressing the core security goal of preventing a nuclear-armed Iran.

Despite retracting its discredited gang rape story, Rolling Stone’s reporting highlighted that the University of Virginia has never expelled a student for sexual assault. The university now faces ongoing investigations by the Virginia attorney general and the U.S. Department of Education into its handling of campus sexual violence allegations. Critics warn the retraction may discourage victims from coming forward, even as it underscored systemic failures in UVA’s response to such cases.

Indiana Pacers forward Chris Copeland was stabbed in New York City early Wednesday, leaving him and two women injured. Atlanta Hawks teammates Pero Antic and Thabo Sefolosha were arrested on obstruction charges after interfering with police at the scene, though they were not involved in the attack. Copeland is in stable condition while a suspect remains in custody pending charges.

Twisted Sister announced its 2016 "Forty and F*ck It" tour will be its final run, marking the band's 40th anniversary. The farewell series features new drummer Mike Portnoy replacing the late A.J. Pero, with two tribute shows dedicated to his memory.

John Travolta dismissed HBO’s critical Scientology documentary "Going Clear," stating he has no interest in viewing the film due to his positive 40-year experience with the church. The actor attributed the project to disgruntled former members and credited Scientology with helping him survive his son’s death.

"Furious 7" earned a record $146 million opening weekend, driven by an emotional tribute to late star Paul Walker that resonated deeply with audiences. Director James Wan opted to retire Walker's character rather than kill him off, utilizing body doubles and CGI to craft a sincere farewell. Social media reactions praised the poignant ending and accompanying Wiz Khalifa song as a fitting homage to the actor.

"Game of Thrones" returns for its fifth season with a simultaneous global premiere across 170 countries, marking the first time major plotlines advance beyond George R.R. Martin's published books. Key story arcs will converge as Tyrion meets Daenerys and Stannis clashes with the Night's Watch, while producers promise escalating drama and battles. The season also shifts focus to the Stark daughters, Cersei, and the growing unrest among Westeros' common folk.

Recent accounts highlight rare survival stories of individuals stranded at sea for weeks or months, relying on ingenuity and luck to endure extreme conditions. Cases include a fisherman adrift for over a year in the Pacific and others rescued after capsizing or engine failures left them isolated from help. These incidents underscore the high mortality rate of such ordeals, with survivors often attributing their rescue to resourcefulness and faith.

The first six "Star Wars" films arrive on digital HD Friday, featuring extensive behind-the-scenes content on sound design. Exclusive materials include a look at how animal sounds were used to create the voices of the Geonosians.

Jurors convicted Dzhokhar Tsarnaev on all 30 counts for the 2013 Boston Marathon bombings, bringing a measure of accountability to survivors and victims' families. While many expressed relief and gratitude for the verdict, they emphasized that true justice remains elusive and the path to healing continues. The ruling marks a pivotal step toward closure for the community, reaffirming resilience in the face of terrorism.
China has formally charged former security czar Zhou Yongk

A Philadelphia mother faces multiple charges, including aggravated assault and kidnapping, for allegedly abandoning her quadriplegic son in a park for four days to visit a boyfriend in Maryland. The 21-year-old victim suffered dehydration and exposure before being discovered by authorities, while his mother lied about his whereabouts. She remains in custody pending extradition to Pennsylvania as investigators examine potential systemic failures in his care.

Walmart’s opposition to Arkansas’ religious freedom bill helped force Governor Asa Hutchinson to demand amendments, signaling the retailer's growing influence as a bellwether for shifting public opinion on gay rights. The move aligns Walmart with a broader corporate backlash against similar legislation in Indiana, pressuring Republican leaders to reconcile religious liberty claims with nondiscrimination standards. This stance highlights a strategic pivot by major businesses toward inclusive policies, urging the GOP to adapt to evolving middle-class values.

A lapsed Catholic describes how Pope Francis’s compassionate tone and refusal to judge have reawakened their faith after years of feeling rejected by church bureaucracy. Cardinal Gerald Lacroix reinforces this shift, emphasizing a welcoming approach that prioritizes Gospel foundations over rigid exclusion. The author concludes with a renewed commitment to attend Mass, inspired by the Pontiff’s message of inclusion rather than imposition.

Mary Kay Letourneau Fualaau and Vili Fualaau defend their marriage in an upcoming ABC interview ahead of their 10th anniversary. Letourneau, who served prison time for her affair with Fualaau when he was a minor, reveals plans to return to teaching and seek removal from the sex offender registry.

Hillary Clinton’s 2016 presidential bid places an unfair burden on her to serve as the sole barometer for U.S. gender equality. The author argues that partisan dynamics and economic factors, rather than systemic sexism, will ultimately determine the election's outcome. Consequently, interpreting her potential victory or defeat as a definitive referendum on women in politics remains a flawed and risky endeavor.

Amnesty International reports a 22% global drop in executions for 2014, even as governments increasingly leverage the death penalty to combat perceived terrorism threats. Conversely, death sentences surged by 28% due to mass sentencing in nations like Egypt and Nigeria, often following unfair trials. While long-term trends favor abolition, China, Iran, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia remain the world's leading executioners.

Japan's Defense Minister Gen Nakatani confirmed to parliament that the Air Self-Defense Force has never encountered extraterrestrial UFOs. The statement responded to a query from lawmaker Antonio Inoki regarding potential alien threats and ongoing research into visitors from outer space.

Mark Wahlberg will star in and produce "Patriots' Day," a CBS Films drama depicting the Boston Marathon bombing manhunt from Police Commissioner Ed Davis's perspective. The project utilizes research from CBS News' "60 Minutes" and marks the second major film announced about the 2013 attack.

Democratic presidential hopefuls Martin O'Malley and Jim Webb displayed contrasting campaign styles at an Iowa event, with O'Malley actively engaging voters while the more stoic Webb focused on policy issues. Both candidates face steep odds against front-runner Hillary Clinton, polling at just 1-3% in early surveys. Despite their differences, both men emphasized their commitment to campaigning in key early voting states.

Turkish authorities arrested nine British citizens, including four children, at the Syria border on suspicion of attempting an illegal crossing. The group, holding valid UK passports, was detained amid ongoing concerns regarding Western recruitment by ISIS and other extremist factions in the region. The British Foreign Office confirmed awareness of the incident and is currently seeking further details from Turkish officials.

The U.S. Department of Justice has indicted FedEx on 15 criminal counts, alleging the courier service knowingly facilitated illegal prescription drug distribution despite prior warnings from federal agencies. FedEx maintains its innocence, arguing it qualifies for a "common carrier" exemption that protects transporters unaware of package contents from possession charges. The case highlights the legal complexities of corporate criminal liability and the government's strategy of targeting supply chains to combat the illicit pharmaceutical market.

Kenyans mourned 147 victims of the Garissa University massacre through social media tributes and Easter services, marking the nation's deadliest terror attack since 1998. Al-Shabaab gunmen targeted Christian students in the assault, while authorities identified one slain attacker as the son of a local government chief.

Photographer Johan Bavman documents Swedish fathers utilizing the nation's generous parental leave policy, which mandates shared "daddy months" to promote gender equality. Despite incentives, only 12% of couples share leave equally, yet Bavman’s project highlights the deep bonding and domestic realities experienced by participating dads. The ongoing series aims to feature 60 fathers in an upcoming exhibition and book challenging traditional parenting roles.

President Obama pledged to maintain Israel’s military edge and defend it against attacks while defending the U.S.-led nuclear deal with Iran. The commitment comes amid sharp criticism from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and congressional Republicans regarding the agreement's safeguards. Negotiations on the final draft continue until June 30 as the administration argues the deal prevents Iranian nuclear weapon development through strict inspections.

Amidst backlash over Indiana's new Religious Freedom Restoration Act, experts note that similar state laws have yielded few legal victories, primarily benefiting religious minorities rather than Christian denominations. Key precedents include Supreme Court protections for Native American eagle feathers and Brazilian sacramental tea, alongside settlements for Sikh and Jewish practitioners. Conversely, courts have rejected some claims, such as a Chicago church group's challenge to zoning laws, highlighting the limited scope of these religious liberty provisions.

Chinese prosecutors face a Monday deadline to decide on formal charges against five detained feminists, who could receive up to five years in prison for "assembling a crowd to disturb public order." The activists were arrested before International Women's Day while planning anti-harassment campaigns, sparking international condemnation and calls for their release from rights groups and global figures.

Selena’s family is partnering with tech firm Acrovirt LLC to create "Selena the One," an autonomous digital embodiment of the late singer set to debut in 2018. The project aims to expand her legacy through new music, collaborations, and a tour, distinguishing itself from previous hologram performances with advanced interactive technology. An Indiegogo campaign launching April 16 seeks $500,000 to support the initiative.

Former Rep. Michele Bachmann sparked backlash by comparing President Obama to the Germanwings co-pilot, labeling him a "deranged pilot" steering the U.S. toward disaster via the Iran nuclear deal. Critics condemned the remark as disrespectful and desperate amid ongoing negotiations to restrict Tehran's nuclear program.

Ryan Gosling’s divisive directorial debut "Lost River" uses decaying Detroit as a central character, capturing the city's ruin and resilience through a post-industrial gothic lens. The film originated from Gosling’s urgent desire to document the Brewster-Douglass Projects before their demolition, evolving into a narrative balancing destruction with signs of urban rebirth. Despite mixed critical reception, the project highlights Detroit’s paradoxical state of annihilation and regeneration ahead of its limited theatrical release.

A 19-year-old UK national was charged with terror offenses Wednesday after being arrested at Luton Airport upon his return from Turkey. Yahya Rashid faces counts of preparing for and assisting acts of terrorism related to conduct between November and March. He is scheduled to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court later today.

Mötley Crüe’s Vince Neil joins a roster of celebrities who faced public backlash for botched renditions of "The Star-Spangled Banner." Historical precedents range from Whitney Houston’s acclaimed Super Bowl performance to Roseanne Barr’s presidential condemnation and Michael Bolton’s lyric flub. These incidents underscore the high stakes and polarizing nature of performing the U.S. national anthem.

Nearly 2,000 World War I soldier inscriptions have been discovered in a sealed underground quarry near Naours, France, offering a rare glimpse into the lives of troops stationed near the Battle of the Somme. Photographer Jeff Gusky documented the site after its 2013 transfer to local authorities, identifying names from Australian, British, and American units among the well-preserved graffiti. The find provides a poignant human connection to the conflict, with many soldiers recording their identities shortly before facing combat.

The Palestinian Authority officially became the 123rd member of the International Criminal Court on Wednesday, granting the body jurisdiction over alleged crimes in Palestinian territories since June 2014. The move, opposed by Israel and the United States, paves the way for potential war crimes investigations against both Palestinians and Israelis.

Anthony Ray Hinton was released from Alabama's death row Friday after nearly 30 years, following a judge's dismissal of murder charges due to flawed forensic evidence. The state declined to retry the case after experts testified the gun linked to Hinton could not be matched to the 1985 crimes. Hinton maintained his innocence throughout his incarceration, citing systemic injustice and inadequate legal representation as key factors in his wrongful conviction.

Most Americans overlook the U.S. tax system's structural inequities, favoring wage earners over the wealthy, due to the psychological impact of receiving large annual refunds. This "happy ending" transforms Tax Day into a spending spree, effectively masking deep-seated legislative biases and complexity. Consequently, public focus remains on immediate financial gain rather than addressing systemic unfairness.

Jordan Spieth maintained a four-shot lead heading into the final round of the 2015 Masters despite a late double bogey on Saturday. Chasing pack contenders Phil Mickelson, Justin Rose, Tiger Woods, and Rory McIlroy failed to significantly close the gap during "Moving Day." Spieth remains the favorite to win, holding a commanding advantage over the field at Augusta National.

Liana Barrientos pleaded not guilty to felony charges for allegedly lying on a 2010 marriage license as part of an immigration fraud scheme involving ten marriages. Prosecutors assert the serial bride wed multiple men simultaneously to help them secure U.S. residency, with divorces finalized only after applications were approved. Barrientos faces up to four years in prison if convicted, with her next court date set for May 18.

Indiana's Memories Pizza sparked national controversy and boycotts after owners stated they would refuse to cater same-sex weddings under the state's Religious Freedom Restoration Act. Despite online harassment and threats that temporarily closed the business, supporters rallied to donate over $842,000 via a crowdfunding campaign.

Vijay Chokalingam, brother of actress Mindy Kaling, sparked controversy by revealing he fraudulently applied to medical school as African-American to protest affirmative action policies. Despite securing multiple interviews, he received only one acceptance offer and faced racial profiling, undermining his claim that minorities receive unearned privilege. Critics argue his stunt ignored the systemic burdens of racism and the necessity of diversity initiatives in addressing healthcare disparities.

Antarctica’s Esperanza Base recorded a potential record high of 63.5°F on March 24, prompting the World Meteorological Organization to launch an official verification process. An expert committee will assess equipment and procedures before issuing a final ruling on the measurement by late summer or early fall.

The Obama administration has abandoned specific timelines for an Iraqi-led offensive to retake Mosul from ISIS, citing the operation's complexity and need for further capacity building. While coalition airstrikes continue and recent gains in Tikrit signal progress, officials emphasize that a ground assault on the strategic northern city is not imminent.

Irish bookmaker Paddy Power deleted a controversial tweet comparing Newcastle United's losses to police killings of unarmed African-Americans, sparking widespread public outrage. The company defended the post as an ill-judged joke ahead of Liverpool's 2-0 Premier League victory over Newcastle. Social media users condemned the remark, with some calling for the dismissal of the employee responsible.

Philadelphia police have added attempted murder charges against Nyia Parler for abandoning her quadriplegic son in a park for four days. Parler remains in Maryland custody for unspecified treatment and cannot be extradited until it is completed. The victim suffered dehydration and exposure but is recovering in a Philadelphia hospital.

South Korean authorities have charged Kim Ki-Jong with attempted murder for the March 5 stabbing of U.S. Ambassador Mark Lippert in Seoul. The indictment, which also includes charges of assaulting a foreign envoy, mandates that Kim’s trial begin within 14 days.

Jill Duggar Dillard, the first married daughter from "19 Kids and Counting," gave birth to a son named Israel David on Monday. The 9-pound, 10-ounce baby arrived more than a week past his due date, as confirmed by People magazine and the family's Facebook page.

"Furious 7" is projected to debut with $135 million-$138 million domestically, marking the largest North American opening since late 2013. The film, serving as Paul Walker's final appearance, is also on track for a global launch approaching $300 million across a record-wide international release.

The Secret Service has placed supervisor Xavier Morales on administrative leave following allegations he sexually assaulted a female employee at a work celebration. Director Joe Clancy condemned the "very disturbing" incident as the agency continues to grapple with a series of recent high-profile security lapses and leadership scandals. The Office of the Inspector General will conduct a further investigation into the matter.

Hillary Clinton officially enters the 2016 presidential race, leveraging extensive political experience and strong poll numbers despite lingering concerns over authenticity and trust. To avoid the pitfalls of her 2008 campaign and Al Gore’s 2000 bid, she must energize the Democratic base with a clear policy vision rather than relying on inevitability. Her path forward requires navigating challenges including gender bias, skepticism from progressive voters, and potential liabilities associated with her husband and the Clinton Foundation.

The Department of Justice will negotiate with Ferguson to restructure its police department following a report citing systemic racial discrimination and predatory court practices. Recent elections have shifted the city council’s racial composition, while key officials including the police chief and town manager have resigned amid ongoing unrest. Activists now face the critical task of influencing these negotiations to ensure substantive reform rather than superficial changes.

Etihad Airways is searching for a missing cat that escaped its damaged carrier upon arrival at New York's JFK Airport. The airline has engaged third-party specialists and airport officials to locate the pet, stating it will review handling procedures following the incident. Owner Jennifer Stewart continues the search with detection dogs and traps, expressing devastation over the loss.

Louis Jordan, 37, was rescued by a container ship crew after drifting for 66 days on his damaged sailboat off the U.S. East Coast. Despite capsizing multiple times and enduring severe storms, Jordan survived by catching fish with his laundry and collecting rainwater. He was hospitalized in Norfolk, Virginia, in surprisingly good physical condition given the ordeal.
